items.title: ONE token turned a $0.40 AI request into $0.80.
items.summary:
ONE token turned a $0.40 AI request into $0.80.

and 4 "cheap" $20 subscriptions quietly cost $1,080 a year.

so i wrote 98 lines of python to audit what AI actually costs. real published prices, no vibes.

it said cut $360. the cache line alone was -88%.

here's what nobody checks.

ChatGPT Plus $20. Claude Pro $20. SuperGrok $30. Cursor Pro $20.
$90 a month. $1,080 a year. before tax.

each one looks reasonable the day you click subscribe. the bill only shows up when they stack

what the script printed, prices as of Aug 28, US web:

> 5M input + 1M output tokens a month: Sonnet 5 $20.00, Grok 4.6 $16.00, GPT-5.6 Luna $2.20
> use 1/5 of that and Sonnet is $4. not $20
> keep 2 subs + a $20 API budget: $720/yr. saves $360
> agent sending the same 100K prompt 50 times: $10.00 naive, $1.23 cached. -88%
> batch API: half price if you can wait
> Grok 4.6 at 199,999 tokens: $0.40. at 200,000: $0.80. one token doubles the whole request
> 20K records to JSON: $160 on Sol, $8.80 on Luna (my assumption: 1K in / 200 out each)

the lesson isn't "API is cheaper". heavy users burn $20 of API in days. the lesson is most people never did the math

how to audit yours:
1. list every AI sub and what you actually use it for
2. split the product (IDE, bots, connectors) from the model access
3. log 30 days of how often you open each one
4. move the occasional ones to pay-per-token
5. cache stable prompts, batch what can wait, watch the 200K / 272K cliffs
6. route easy work to cheap models, keep the frontier one for hard problems

every subscription has to earn its spot on your card. my math on published prices, not financial advice

In an interview with Fortune, Wang explained that, even at a time when there are a multitude of so-called Layer 1 blockchains, he chose to build another because he believes blockchain is the best technology for transferring money. He added that none of the existing options offer a set of privacy and compliance tools designed for banks and other large financial players. [...] Financial firms looking to accelerate money transfers with crypto have no shortage of options when it comes to blockchains, including Ethereum, Solana and Avalanche. That hasn’t deterred a startup called Alta from trying to lure banks and big companies with a blockchain of its own. The chain seeks to stand out with its plug-and-play compliance layer that lets customers ensure that any transactions they process are consistent with rules and regulations anywhere in the world.

Recommended Video [...] “We often say we wouldn’t have built an L-1 if we didn’t have to,” said Wang, noting that Alta’s features include one that prevents random people from sending funds to those with an address on the blockchain. (Most blockchains allow for so-called “airdrops” that oblige wallet holders to accept funds whether they want to or not).

items.title: OpenAI Acquires Odessia, travel startup created by Sonder founder | TechCrunch
items.summary:
OpenAI did not announce this acquisition, nor confirm it to TechCrunch, when asked. Nor has it announced new travel-specific products or plans. It does, however, count such companies as Bookings.com, Expedia, and KAYAK as customers or partners.

Travel is one of the main areas that people are using personal AI assistants to help with. And, back in July, 2025, when OpenAI launched its ChatGPT agent, it mentioned travel as one of its potential uses. [...] OpenAI has acquired an AI travel agent called Odessia, according to Odessia’s founder, Francis Davidson. Davidson says in a post announcing the deal that he’s now working for OpenAI, helping the AI lab with the future of travel. [...] So we’ll have to wait and see what OpenAI has in store now, with his joining the company. OpenAI has not yet responded to a request for comment.
